To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a network of excitatoriy and inhibitory model neuron with a sparse and random connectivity can perform information processing tasks in an efficient way if the noise level is moderate.
the information buffering capacity of sparsely connected networks of integrate-and fire neurons depends on the amount of noise and on the correlation of the input signal.
the information buffering performance of a sparsely connected network of integrate-and-fire model neurons is best for moderate noise levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of noise and signal correlations in a network of model neurons and their influence on information transfer and storage.

the analysis of transient information storage in a network of integrate-and-fire model neurons with excitatory and inhibtory synapses and with the investigation of the role of noise for information buffering.
the question, whether and how the brain can process information in the ultra-short term, i.e., on the order of a millisecond or less.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
noise is not a nuisance but a necessary condition for the performance of information processing in a sparsely-connected network of integrate-and-fire model neurons.
the network is able to store information in the form of a population code for a short time period.
the network performs well in a narrow band of noise levels around the transition between quiescence and stochastic dynamics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the network can buffer information for a time that scales linearly with the number of neurons.
the optimal performance is reached for the network in a state between quiescence and stochastic dynamics, and that this optimal performance is achieved for a moderate, but non-zero amount of noise.
we have investigated the role of signal autocorrelation in a sparsely-connected network of integrate-and-fire model neurons for transient information processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a network with sparse excitatory and inhibi- tory connections can be used as a buffer for ultra-short term storage of information in a regime of asynchronous irregular firing, which is the most realistic regime in terms of the dynamics of cortical micro-circuit models.

for the case of ultra-short term information storage and processing the performance of networks of integrate-and fire neurons is determined by the amount of noise in the system and by the correlation properties of the input signals.
information processing can be enhanced by noise in a network of neurons.
